Liberalism puts the individual first — freedom, reason, toleration and a state built on consent.
It was revolutionary because it overthrew feudal privilege and the divine right of kings.
It evolved: classical (minimal state, Smith/Locke) → modern/welfare (positive liberty, Green) → neo-liberal (roll back the state, Hayek/Friedman).
Neo-liberalism became globalization’s ideology (Thatcher, Reagan, WTO, Washington Consensus).

Q — Critically examine postmodernism’s ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’ alongside the ‘end of ideology’ and ‘end of history’ theses. (UPSC 2017)
Postmodernism distrusts all ‘grand theories’ (like Marxism or liberalism) that claim one universal truth.
Lyotard: postmodernism = ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’; there are many truths, not one.
‘End of ideology’ (Bell): after WWII the big ideological battles died down in a welfare-capitalist consensus.
‘End of history’ (Fukuyama): after the Cold War, liberal democracy won — but both theses were overtaken by new conflicts.

All three theses proclaim an ‘end’ to universal truth or ideological struggle, yet the persistence of nationalism, religion and inequality refutes them. Postmodernism usefully warns against dogmatic metanarratives, but its own relativism risks leaving no ground on which to criticise injustice.
Q — Distinguish revolutionary from evolutionary socialism; assess pre-Marxist (utopian) socialism and whether socialism may be reborn as anti-capitalism. (UPSC 2015/2014)
Socialism’s core value is social/economic equality and cooperation over competition.
Revolutionary socialism (Marx): overthrow capitalism in one stroke; Evolutionary socialism: reach it gradually through the ballot and reform.
Pre-Marx ‘utopian’ socialists (Owen, Fourier, Saint-Simon) dreamed of ideal communities but had no scientific programme.

Q — Explain the main tenets of Marxism (dialectical and historical materialism, class conflict, surplus value) and evaluate its contemporary relevance. (UPSC 2019)

Class struggle drives history; capitalism exploits workers by pocketing ‘surplus value’.

Q — Why is the sex/gender distinction central to feminist analysis? Distinguish liberal, socialist and radical feminism and the waves of feminism. (UPSC 2012/2019)
Sex is biological (unchangeable); gender is the social role ‘made’ by society (changeable) — so women’s subordination is not natural.
This lets feminists reject ‘biology is destiny’ and demand change.
Liberal feminism = equal rights within the system; socialist = link patriarchy to capitalism; radical = patriarchy is the deepest oppression.
Three waves: 1st = suffrage/legal rights; 2nd = ‘women’s liberation’/private sphere; 3rd = difference and diversity.

Q — “One is not born, but becomes, a woman.” Examine radical feminism and patriarchy, and evaluate eco-feminism and the newer strands (black, postcolonial). (UPSC 2017)
Radical feminism says patriarchy — male domination — is the oldest and deepest form of oppression, rooted in the family and sexuality.
It coined ‘the personal is political’: private life (marriage, sex, housework) is a site of power.

Q — Is fascism a coherent ideology? Discuss its anti-rationalism and core tenets, its conception of the state, and whether it was merely an inter-war phenomenon.
Fascism glorifies the nation/state and the leader above the individual — ‘the individual is nothing’.
It is anti-rational: it exalts will, struggle, war and myth over reason (‘1789 is dead’).
Core tenets: struggle/social Darwinism, leader-worship, ultranationalism, totalitarian corporatist state.
It is not a coherent doctrine (a ‘hodge-podge’); Marxists (Laski) call it ‘capitalism defending itself’.

contentText: Syllabus — Political Ideologies: Liberalism, Socialism, Marxism, Fascism, Gandhism, Feminism. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 8) [Gandhism is treated fully in Unit 9.] Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  the major political ideologies — Liberalism (classical, modern, neo-liberal), Socialism (utopian, revolutionary, evolutionary), Marxism (classical and neo-Marxism), Feminism (its waves and strands) and Fascism — together with Postmodernism and the ‘end of ideology’ and ‘end of history’ debates. Gandhism is covered in Unit 9. Must-know thinkers:  Locke, Adam Smith, T.H. Green, Hayek, Nozick, Friedman, Rawls, Sen, Lyotard, Foucault, Robert Owen, Bernstein, G.B. Shaw (Fabians), Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao, Gramsci, Marcuse, Althusser, Wollstonecraft, Beauvoir, Betty Friedan, Kate Millett, Mussolini, Hitler, Gentile. PYQ trend:  liberalism as a revolutionary idea (2020), end of history (2017), pre-Marxist socialism (2015) & socialism as anti-capitalism (2014), relevance of Marxism (2019), liberal vs radical feminism (2012/2019) & eco-feminism (2017), fascist anti-rationalism, postmodernism (2017). Master Questions Q — Trace the evolution of liberalism from classical to modern to neo-liberalism. Was liberalism a revolutionary idea, and is neo-liberalism the ideology of globalization? (UPSC 2020) Gist — the spine to recall Liberalism puts the individual first — freedom, reason, toleration and a state built on consent. It was revolutionary because it overthrew feudal privilege and the divine right of kings. It evolved: classical (minimal state, Smith/Locke) → modern/welfare (positive liberty, Green) → neo-liberal (roll back the state, Hayek/Friedman). Neo-liberalism became globalization’s ideology (Thatcher, Reagan, WTO, Washington Consensus). Model Answer Liberalism is a  meta-ideology  built on a commitment to the individual, with five core values —  individualism, freedom, reason, justice and toleration . It was  revolutionary  in its day: by grounding legitimate rule in the  consent of the people , it overthrew feudal privilege and the divine right of kings. Classical liberalism  ( Locke  — ‘father of classical liberalism’,  Adam Smith, Herbert Spencer ) champions a minimal ‘night-watchman’ state, laissez-faire, natural rights and  negative liberty ;  Jefferson : ‘that government is best which governs least’.  Macpherson  labels its individual ‘possessive’. Modern / positive liberalism  ( T.H. Green, Hobhouse, Laski ) makes the state a ‘source of virtue’ enabling  positive liberty : Green — ‘will, not force, is the basis of the state’, the state ‘hinders the hindrances’ to self-development, justifying the welfare state. Neo-liberalism  ( Hayek, Nozick, Friedman ) reverses this — ‘rolling back the state’ and ‘market fundamentalism’.  Hayek : ‘planning is the road to serfdom’, ‘social justice is a mirage’;  Friedman : freedom is possible only through the market. It became the ideology of globalization — Thatcherism/Reaganism, shock therapy, the WTO (1995) and the  Washington Consensus . Conclusion.  Liberalism was a genuinely revolutionary force against absolutism, and it renews itself through  social liberalism  ( Rawls, Sen, Stiglitz ), which revives positive liberty against neo-liberal excess — showing liberalism’s capacity to adapt from market-freedom to ‘humane governance’. Q — Critically examine postmodernism’s ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’ alongside the ‘end of ideology’ and ‘end of history’ theses. (UPSC 2017) Gist — the spine to recall Postmodernism distrusts all ‘grand theories’ (like Marxism or liberalism) that claim one universal truth. Lyotard: postmodernism = ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’; there are many truths, not one. ‘End of ideology’ (Bell): after WWII the big ideological battles died down in a welfare-capitalist consensus. ‘End of history’ (Fukuyama): after the Cold War, liberal democracy won — but both theses were overtaken by new conflicts. Model Answer Postmodernism is a rejection of Modernism that ‘emphasises the elusiveness of meaning and knowledge’;  Nietzsche  is regarded as its father (‘God is dead’, ‘will to power’).  Jean-Francois Lyotard  gave its defining formula: postmodernism is  ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’  — disbelief in any grand, universal theory, for ‘there is not one but many truths’. Its key moves:  Foucault’s  ‘power/knowledge’ (‘we do not discover truth, we invent truth’);  Derrida’s   deconstruction  of the ‘metaphysics of presence’; and  Baudrillard’s  ‘hyper-reality’ where media becomes more real than reality. End of ideology.  Daniel Bell  (with  Lipset, Dahrendorf ) argued that after the Second World War the great ideological conflicts had exhausted themselves — ‘economics triumphed over politics’ in a welfare-capitalist consensus. Critics ( Macpherson, MacIntyre ) replied that ‘the end of ideology is itself an ideology’. End of history.  Francis Fukuyama  extended this after the Cold War: the ‘worldwide triumph of liberal democracy’ over all rivals (a Hegelian idea).  Samuel Huntington  countered with the ‘clash of civilizations’ — ethnic and religious identity, not ideology, would drive future conflict. Conclusion.  All three theses proclaim an ‘end’ to universal truth or ideological struggle, yet the persistence of nationalism, religion and inequality refutes them. Postmodernism usefully warns against dogmatic metanarratives, but its own relativism risks leaving no ground on which to criticise injustice. Q — Distinguish revolutionary from evolutionary socialism; assess pre-Marxist (utopian) socialism and whether socialism may be reborn as anti-capitalism. (UPSC 2015/2014) Gist — the spine to recall Socialism’s core value is social/economic equality and cooperation over competition. Revolutionary socialism (Marx): overthrow capitalism in one stroke; Evolutionary socialism: reach it gradually through the ballot and reform. Pre-Marx ‘utopian’ socialists (Owen, Fourier, Saint-Simon) dreamed of ideal communities but had no scientific programme. Today socialism revives as anti-capitalism (Occupy, inequality debates) — ‘socialism or barbarism’ (Wallerstein). Model Answer Socialism is defined by its opposition to capitalism; its ‘defining value is equality, especially social equality’, and cooperation over competition.  C.E.M. Joad  quipped that ‘socialism is like a hat that has lost its shape because everyone wears it’. Pre-Marxist / utopian socialism.  Robert Owen  (who first used ‘socialist’) proposed ‘villages of cooperation’;  Charles Fourier  wanted to make work pleasant;  Saint-Simon  favoured rule by scientific ‘luminaries’. Marx called them  ‘utopian’  because they painted ideal futures without a scientific analysis of capitalism or a programme to get there. Revolutionary vs evolutionary.  Revolutionary socialism  (the Marxist tradition) seeks to overthrow capitalism ‘in a single stroke’ for a classless society.  Evolutionary socialism  (the liberal/‘democratic socialist’ tradition) proceeds gradually and parliamentarily:  revisionism  ( Bernstein  — workers with the vote need no revolution),  Fabianism  ( G.B. Shaw, the Webbs ; inspiration for Nehruvian socialism),  syndicalism  and  guild socialism  ( G.D.H. Cole ). Rebirth as anti-capitalism.  With inequality rising, socialism revives as an anti-capitalist critique —  Ralph Miliband’s   Socialism for a Sceptical Age , movements like Occupy Wall Street and the Yellow Vests, and  Wallerstein’s  stark choice, ‘socialism or barbarism’. Conclusion.  Evolutionary socialism made socialism democratically respectable but is charged with legitimising the bourgeois state (a ‘safety valve’); its 21st-century relevance lies less in seizing power than in supplying the moral vocabulary of the fight against inequality — socialism reborn as anti-capitalism. Q — Explain the main tenets of Marxism (dialectical and historical materialism, class conflict, surplus value) and evaluate its contemporary relevance. (UPSC 2019) Gist — the spine to recall Marxism is the ‘scientific’ theory of socialism: history is driven by class conflict over who owns production. Dialectical materialism: reality is matter in conflict (thesis-antithesis-synthesis); historical materialism: the economic ‘base’ shapes the ‘superstructure’. Class struggle drives history; capitalism exploits workers by pocketing ‘surplus value’. Relevance: inequality, 2008 crisis and Occupy revive it (Piketty, Eagleton) — though its predictions largely failed. Model Answer Marxism, founded by  Marx  and  Engels , claims to give socialism a ‘scientific’ basis, treating history as the conflict of antagonistic classes. Dialectical materialism  fuses  Hegel’s  dialectic (thesis–antithesis–synthesis) with materialism — matter, not idea, is the essence of reality;  Engels  gives its three laws.  Historical materialism  applies this to society: the economic  base  (mode of production) determines the  superstructure  (law, politics, ideas), driving history through stages — slave → feudal → capitalist → socialist → communist. Class struggle and surplus value.  ‘The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggle’; the proletariat is ‘the only really revolutionary class’. Capitalism exploits workers through  surplus value  — labour alone creates value, but the capitalist pockets the unpaid surplus. When the ‘class in itself’ becomes a ‘class for itself’, revolution follows. Contemporary relevance.  Marxism’s predictions (imminent revolution, immiseration) largely failed, and state-socialist regimes collapsed. Yet its  critique of capitalism  endures:  Thomas Piketty  ( Capital in the Twenty-First Century ) documents widening inequality,  Terry Eagleton  ( Why Marx Was Right ) defends its core, and movements like Occupy Wall Street echo its concerns. Conclusion.  As a blueprint for revolution Marxism has been largely discredited; as a  diagnostic tool  for exploitation, alienation and inequality under capitalism it remains strikingly relevant — which is why each crisis of capitalism renews interest in Marx. Q — How did neo-Marxism (Gramsci, the Frankfurt School, Althusser) reformulate the base–superstructure relationship? Gist — the spine to recall Classical Marxism said the economy (base) simply determines everything else (superstructure). Neo-Marxists said culture and ideas have their own power — that’s why workers didn’t revolt. Gramsci: the ruling class rules by ‘hegemony’ (consent), so revolution needs a ‘war of position’ in the realm of ideas. Frankfurt School (Marcuse’s ‘one-dimensional man’) and Althusser (ideological state apparatuses) deepened this cultural turn. Model Answer Classical Marxism treated the  superstructure  (ideas, law, culture, the state) as a mere reflection of the economic  base . When revolution failed to arrive in the advanced West,  neo-Marxists  rescued Marxism from this ‘crude economic determinism’ by giving the superstructure real autonomy. Antonio Gramsci , the ‘theoretician of the superstructure’, argued the ruling class rules not just by coercion but by  hegemony  — manufacturing consent through  civil society  (school, church, media), so the exploited accept their exploitation as ‘common sense’. Revolution therefore needs first a  war of position  — an ideological struggle led by  organic intellectuals  to build counter-hegemony — before the physical ‘war of manoeuvre’. The  Frankfurt School  ( Horkheimer, Adorno, Marcuse ) developed  critical theory  and the idea of the ‘culture industry’;  Marcuse’s   One-Dimensional Man  shows how capitalism manufactures ‘false needs’ that absorb dissent. Louis Althusser  (the structuralist school) added the  ‘ideological state apparatuses’  and  interpellation  (ideology ‘hails’ individuals into subjects), and a ‘multi-sectoral’ analysis rejecting economic determinism — the base is determinant only ‘in the last instance’. Conclusion.  Neo-Marxism shifted the decisive battleground from the  economy to culture and consciousness  — explaining capitalism’s durability and reshaping Marxism into a theory of ideology and hegemony rather than of inevitable economic collapse. Q — Why is the sex/gender distinction central to feminist analysis? Distinguish liberal, socialist and radical feminism and the waves of feminism. (UPSC 2012/2019) Gist — the spine to recall Sex is biological (unchangeable); gender is the social role ‘made’ by society (changeable) — so women’s subordination is not natural. This lets feminists reject ‘biology is destiny’ and demand change. Liberal feminism = equal rights within the system; socialist = link patriarchy to capitalism; radical = patriarchy is the deepest oppression. Three waves: 1st = suffrage/legal rights; 2nd = ‘women’s liberation’/private sphere; 3rd = difference and diversity. Model Answer Feminist ideology rests on two beliefs — ‘that women are disadvantaged because of their sex, and that this disadvantage can and should be overthrown’. The  sex/gender distinction  is central because  sex  is biological and fixed, whereas  gender  is a cultural construct that can be changed — as  Simone de Beauvoir  put it, ‘one is not born, but becomes, a woman’. This shatters the claim that ‘biology is destiny’ and makes subordination a social wrong to be corrected. Liberal feminism  ( Mary Wollstonecraft ,  A Vindication of the Rights of Woman ;  J.S. Mill ;  Betty Friedan ) is reformist — it seeks equal legal and political rights within the existing system, arguing gender is ‘irrelevant to public life’. Socialist feminism  ( Engels ,  The Origin of the Family ;  Juliet Mitchell ) links patriarchy to  capitalism  — women are a ‘reserve army of labour’ whose unpaid domestic work reproduces labour power.  Radical feminism  ( Kate Millett, Germaine Greer, Beauvoir ) locates the root in  patriarchy  itself — ‘the personal is political’ — reaching into family and sexuality. The three waves.  The  first wave  (to the 1960s) won legal and voting rights (suffrage); the  second wave  (1961–91) was the ‘women’s liberation’ movement targeting the private sphere ( Friedan’s  ‘problem with no name’); the  third wave  (from the 1990s) embraced the politics of difference — black, postcolonial and eco-feminism. Conclusion.  The sex/gender distinction is the theoretical foundation of all feminism because it turns women’s subordination from a fact of nature into a remediable injustice — though the strands differ on whether the cure is equal rights, the end of capitalism, or the overthrow of patriarchy. Q — “One is not born, but becomes, a woman.” Examine radical feminism and patriarchy, and evaluate eco-feminism and the newer strands (black, postcolonial). (UPSC 2017) Gist — the spine to recall Radical feminism says patriarchy — male domination — is the oldest and deepest form of oppression, rooted in the family and sexuality. It coined ‘the personal is political’: private life (marriage, sex, housework) is a site of power. Eco-feminism links the domination of women with the domination of nature (Vandana Shiva). Newer strands (black, postcolonial) say mainstream feminism ignored race and class — not all women are the same. Model Answer Radical feminism, the defining strand of the  second wave , holds that  patriarchy  — ‘rule by men’ — is the most fundamental and universal form of oppression, prior to class or race.  Kate Millett  defines it as a system in which ‘male shall dominate female, elder male shall dominate younger’. Its rallying idea is  ‘the personal is political’ : the private sphere of family, marriage and sexuality is itself a structure of power.  Susan Brownmiller  (‘rape is an institution of patriarchy’) and  Simone de Beauvoir  ( The Second Sex , ‘woman is made, not born’) show how women are constructed as the  ‘Other’ ; some radicals advocate androgyny as the escape. Eco-feminism  (a term credited to  Francoise d’Eaubonne ; developed by  Vandana Shiva  and  Mary Daly ) links the  domination of women  with the  domination of nature  — both treated as passive resources by a masculinist, exploitative order — so women are natural allies of ecology. Newer strands.  Black feminism  ( bell hooks ) and  postcolonial feminism  ( Chandra Talpade Mohanty ) charge that mainstream (white, middle-class) feminism universalised one experience and ignored  race and class ; the ‘third-world woman’ cannot be spoken for by Western feminists. Conclusion.  Radical feminism transformed feminism by politicising the private sphere, but its assumption of a single ‘women’s experience’ — an ‘essential’ femininity — is exactly what eco-, black and postcolonial feminists contest, moving feminism from sisterhood-as-sameness to a  politics of difference . Q — Is fascism a coherent ideology? Discuss its anti-rationalism and core tenets, its conception of the state, and whether it was merely an inter-war phenomenon. Gist — the spine to recall Fascism glorifies the nation/state and the leader above the individual — ‘the individual is nothing’. It is anti-rational: it exalts will, struggle, war and myth over reason (‘1789 is dead’). Core tenets: struggle/social Darwinism, leader-worship, ultranationalism, totalitarian corporatist state. It is not a coherent doctrine (a ‘hodge-podge’); Marxists (Laski) call it ‘capitalism defending itself’. Model Answer Fascism (from  fasces , ‘strength through unity’) subordinates the individual utterly to the nation and state — ‘the individual, in a literal sense, is nothing’ — aiming to forge a ‘new man’. Because it lacks a systematic doctrine it is often called a ‘ hodge-podge of ideologies ’ or a ‘political religion’ rather than a coherent ideology. Anti-rationalism  is its hallmark: a counter-Enlightenment cult of  will, instinct and myth  over reason —  Sorel’s  ‘political myths’, Mussolini’s ‘action not talk’, ‘1789 is dead’. Its other core tenets:  struggle  (social Darwinism — ‘war is to men what maternity is to women’);  leadership and elitism  (the Führerprinzip, Nietzsche’s Übermensch); ‘national socialism’; and chauvinistic  ultranationalism . The state.  Fascism is  totalitarian  and  corporatist  — for  Mussolini  and  Gentile , ‘nothing against the State, nothing over it, nothing beyond it’, drawing on Hegel’s worship of the state. Nazism added  racialism  — Aryan supremacy, anti-Semitism and the ‘final solution’. Merely inter-war?  Ernst Nolte  sees fascism as a product of specific  inter-war circumstances  (defeat, depression, fear of communism), whereas  Erich Fromm  roots it in human nature itself — the ‘fear of freedom’ — implying it can recur.  Laski  (Marxist) calls it ‘a desperate attempt by capitalism to protect itself’. Conclusion.  Fascism is best seen not as a coherent ideology but as a reactive, anti-rational movement of extreme nationalism and leader-worship. Fromm’s ‘fear of freedom’ warns that it was not merely an inter-war accident — its impulses resurface wherever crisis breeds authoritarian nationalism. Revision Box — facts, keywords & quotes Liberalism = meta-ideology;  core values: individualism, freedom, reason, justice, toleration. Liberal phases:  classical (Locke/Smith, night-watchman) → modern (Green, positive liberty) → neo-liberal (Hayek/Nozick/Friedman). Green : ‘will, not force, is the basis of the state’; state ‘hinders the hindrances’. Lyotard : postmodernism = ‘incredulity towards metanarratives’;  Nietzsche  = father of postmodernism. Bell : ‘end of ideology’;  Fukuyama : ‘end of history’;  Huntington : clash of civilizations. Socialism:  Joad — ‘a hat that has lost its shape’; core value = social equality. Utopian socialists:  Owen  (villages of cooperation),  Fourier ,  Saint-Simon . Evolutionary socialism:  revisionism (Bernstein), Fabianism (Shaw/Webbs), syndicalism, guild socialism (Cole). Marxism:  dialectical + historical materialism; base→superstructure; class struggle; surplus value. Marx : ‘history of all society is the history of class struggle’; ‘workers have nothing to lose but their chains’. Neo-Marxism:  Gramsci  (hegemony, war of position), Frankfurt School (Marcuse ‘one-dimensional man’), Althusser (ISAs, interpellation). Feminism:  sex (biological) vs gender (social); Beauvoir — ‘one is not born but becomes a woman’. Feminist strands:  liberal (Wollstonecraft/Mill), socialist (Engels), radical (Millett/Greer); eco-feminism (d’Eaubonne, Shiva). Waves:  1st suffrage; 2nd women’s liberation (Friedan’s ‘problem with no name’); 3rd difference (black/postcolonial). Fascism:  fasces = strength through unity; anti-rationalism; ‘1789 is dead’; totalitarian corporatist state. Laski : fascism = ‘capitalism defending itself’;  Fromm : ‘fear of freedom’;  Nolte : inter-war product.
